Our signal for I am stressed, not angry at you
What I learned from my partner's sheet

title: Brave Words Bank
summary: A child collects the things they can say to themselves when something feels scary or hard.
goal: Give a child their own coping self-talk, in their words, ready before it is needed.
body_md: Collect the words from moments the child has already been brave; ask what they said to themselves then. Add a few from a favorite character or a grown-up they trust. Write them on cards or a poster the child decorates, and have the parent say one back to the child in the moment, not a lecture.

fields.label: A time I was brave, and what I said to myself
Words a favorite character would say
Words my grown-up says that help
My top three brave words
Where my brave words will live
A time this week I used them

title: Social Story Builder
summary: A short, first-person story that walks a child through an upcoming situation step by step.
goal: Take the unknown out of a new or hard situation by rehearsing it in a story the child helps write.
body_md: Write it with the child in the first person and present tense: I walk into the classroom, I find my seat. Include what the child might feel and what they can do, and keep the tone matter-of-fact. Read it daily in the run-up with a parent, and let the child illustrate it. Update it once the real thing has happened.

fields.label: The situation my story is about
What happens first, then next, then next
What I might feel, and what I can do about it
What the grown-ups will be doing
How the story ends
When we will read it, and who with
What really happened, to add to the story

title: Five Senses Hunt Card
summary: A grounding activity turned into a hunt: find five things to see, four to touch, three to hear, two to smell, one to taste.
goal: Teach a child to come back to the room through their senses, as a game they can play anywhere.
body_md: Play it in session with real objects and then in different rooms so it generalizes. Make the card the child's own, with drawings for each sense. Parents run it during big feelings by playing, not instructing: I bet you cannot find four things to touch. Keep a pocket version for school.

fields.label: Five things I can see
Four things I can touch
Three things I can hear
Two things I can smell
One thing I can taste
How my body felt before and after
A place I could play this when I feel wobbly

title: Change Warning Chart
summary: A visual countdown a parent uses before transitions, with the child's chosen warning times and words.
goal: Reduce meltdowns at transitions by making the change visible before it arrives.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Transitions are where many children's hardest moments happen. Build the chart with the child: which changes are hardest, how many warnings they want, and the words that work. The parent gives the warnings the same way every time, with a visible timer where possible. Review the hardest transition after a week.

fields.label: The changes that are hardest for me (stopping play, leaving, bedtime, screens off)
How many warnings I want, and when (ten minutes, five, one)
The words my grown-up will use
What I can do in the last minute to get ready
What helps after the change
How the week's hardest change went

title: Parent Coaching Sheet: Emotion Coaching
summary: The five steps of emotion coaching for a parent to practice on one moment a day.
goal: Help a parent meet a child's feeling before dealing with the behavior.
body_md: The steps are notice the feeling, see it as a chance to connect, listen and validate, name the feeling, and then set limits and problem-solve. Parents usually skip to the last step, so rehearse the middle three in session with a recent example. One coached moment a day is enough to start.

fields.label: The moment I chose today
The feeling I noticed in my child
What I said to show I was listening
The feeling word I offered
The limit I set, after all that
What I found hardest (usually waiting before the limit)
How my child responded

title: Mindful Listening Telephone
summary: A message passed around the circle, but each player must repeat it back to the sender exactly before passing it on.
goal: Make listening a skill players practice under pressure and laughter.
body_md: Start with short messages and lengthen them. A player who repeats it wrong starts the message again from the sender. Round two uses feelings messages: I felt left out when the game changed. The debrief asks what it was like to be repeated back accurately, which is the point.

fields.label: Messages we passed
Where the message broke down, and why
What it felt like to be repeated back exactly
A feelings message I sent
One thing I will do differently when listening this week

title: Yes, And Improv Warm-Up
summary: Partners build a scene one line at a time, each accepting what the other offered and adding to it.
goal: Practice acceptance and flexibility in a playful form before applying them to real life.
body_md: The only rule is that no offer is refused: every line begins by accepting what came before, then adds. Play a round with yes, but first so the group feels the difference. The debrief connects it to life: where the client says no to what is already true, and what yes, and would look like there.

fields.label: A scene we built
What happened when someone said yes, but
What it felt like to have my idea accepted and built on
Where in my life I say no to what is already the case
What yes, and would sound like there

title: Skill Spinner
summary: A spinner or die assigns a coping skill; the player demonstrates it on the spot for a situation card.
goal: Get coping skills rehearsed out loud and on the body rather than remembered as names.
body_md: Fill the spinner with skills the group has actually learned. A player spins, draws a situation, and shows the skill for that situation, with the group judging whether it fits. Misfits are the best teaching moments: a breathing skill spun for a bullying situation opens a conversation about which skill would do.

fields.label: Skills on our spinner
The skill I spun, and the situation I drew
Whether it fit, and what would have fit better
A skill I saw someone else demonstrate well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Feelings Color Draw
summary: Players draw a colored card and name a feeling that color is for them, then a time they felt it.
goal: Reach feelings through color for players who do not yet have the words.
body_md: There are no right answers about which color is which feeling, and the differences between players are worth noticing aloud. A second round asks where in the body the feeling lives. Works well with children who freeze when asked how they feel directly, and as a warm-up for groups.

fields.label: The colors I drew, and the feelings I gave them
A time I felt one of them
A color someone else gave a different feeling to
Where in my body one of my feelings lives
The color I would choose for how I feel right now

title: What Would You Do? Scenario Cards
summary: Scenario cards describing a tricky social or emotional moment, with players giving and then debating their responses.
goal: Rehearse decisions in hard moments while the stakes are only a card.
body_md: Write the scenarios with the group so they are real to them: a friend shares a secret that worries you, someone laughs at your answer, a parent breaks a promise. Each player answers, then the group discusses; there is rarely one right answer, and saying so is part of the game. Keep a few cards for the situations the group finds hardest.

fields.label: Scenarios we wrote
The card I drew, and what I said I would do
An answer from someone else I had not thought of
A scenario the group found hardest
What I would actually do if it happened this week

title: Imposter Thoughts Inventory
summary: Collects the specific thoughts and situations that trigger a sense of being a fraud.
goal: Use it to separate a competence problem from a belief that discounts real evidence of it.
body_md: Ask for concrete recent moments rather than a general feeling. Clients with this pattern tend to credit luck, timing or other people for their wins and remember every stumble in detail, so the evidence columns usually come back lopsided on the first pass. Return to the discounting prompt more than once.

fields.label: A recent moment I felt like a fraud
What I told myself about why it went well anyway
What I would say about someone else in the same position
Evidence of skill or effort I am discounting
Who or what I am comparing myself against
One thing I will let myself take credit for this week

title: Caregiver Load Checklist
summary: Lists the visible and invisible tasks of caring for someone else, and who else could carry each one.
goal: Use it to make an unsustainable caseload of caregiving tasks visible before burnout sets in.
body_md: Include the invisible tasks, the appointments scheduled, the worry carried, the decisions made alone, not only the physical care. Clients in this role often cannot name a single task they could hand off; treat that answer as data rather than the end of the conversation, and come back to it once the full list is on the page.

fields.label: Who I am caring for, and for how long
Physical tasks I do
Mental and emotional tasks I carry
Tasks only I know how to do
Tasks someone else could learn or take over
Who that someone else could be
What has slipped in my own life because of this load

title: Amends and Repair Worksheet
summary: Separates a genuine apology from an explanation, then plans what repair would actually look like.
goal: Use it to turn guilt about a specific action into a concrete repair rather than a general apology.
body_md: Have the client write the apology without the word but, since that word usually turns the sentence into a defense. Separate what they are sorry for from what they wish had happened to them instead. Repair is a specific, offered action, not a promise never to do it again, and the client should be able to say what it costs them.

fields.label: What I did
The impact it had, as best I understand it
My apology, with no but attached
What I am tempted to explain or defend instead
What repair could look like, specifically
What that repair costs me
When I will offer it

title: Screen Time Boundary Planner
summary: Maps when and why a client reaches for a screen, then sets one boundary to try.
goal: Use it to replace a vague goal of using screens less with one specific, timed change.
body_md: Ask what the screen is doing for the client in each moment logged, boredom, avoidance, connection, wind-down, before choosing what to change. A boundary that ignores the function it serves rarely holds. Pick one time and one device rather than an overall reduction, and agree how a slip will be handled without it becoming a failure.

fields.label: When I reach for a screen without deciding to
What it is doing for me in that moment
Where it has crowded out something I wanted
The one boundary I will try
What I will do instead in that moment
How I will handle a slip

title: Chronic Pain Flare Plan
summary: A plan agreed while pain is manageable for what to do when a flare starts.
goal: Use it to replace all-or-nothing reactions to a flare with a prepared, paced response.
body_md: Complete this between flares, not during one, and coordinate with the client’s medical team on anything physical. The pacing prompt matters most: clients with chronic pain often swing between pushing through and doing nothing, and a flare plan should name a middle option they can actually use on a bad day.

fields.label: Early signs that a flare is starting
What tends to trigger a flare for me
What I will scale back first
A middle-ground activity, neither pushing through nor stopping
Who I will tell that I am in a flare
What has helped me recover before
What I will do differently once it passes

title: ABC Model Record
summary: Separates an activating event from the belief about it and the emotional consequence that follows.
goal: Use it to show a client that the event does not directly cause the feeling, the belief in between does.
body_md: Clients almost always describe the event and the feeling fluently and skip the belief, since it usually runs below notice. Slow down there and ask what the event would have to mean for the feeling to make sense. Once the belief is written down plainly, the dispute step in the next session has something specific to work with.

fields.label: Activating event
Belief about the event, as a full sentence
Consequence: the feeling and what I did
How much I believed the belief at the time (0-100%)
A more flexible belief that still takes the event seriously
The feeling now, with the new belief in mind

title: Socratic Questioning Guide
summary: A set of questions a client asks themselves to test a thought rather than accept or fight it.
goal: Use it to give a client a repeatable way to examine a thought without you in the room.
body_md: Model the questions out loud in session first, in your own voice, before handing the sheet over as homework. The point is genuine curiosity rather than a script for arguing the client out of the thought; a client who uses it to attack themselves further needs it slowed down and demonstrated again.

fields.label: The thought I want to examine
What is the evidence for and against it?
Is there another way to look at this?
What would I tell a friend who had this thought?
What is the worst, best and most likely outcome?
Does thinking this way help me, whether or not it is true?
What do I want to do with this thought now?

title: Body Vigilance Diary
summary: Tracks how often and how closely a client is monitoring a body sensation across a day.
goal: Use it to show a client how much checking is feeding a health worry before targeting it directly.
body_md: Health anxiety runs on this kind of checking, and clients are usually unaware of how constant it has become until it is logged. Ask for the checking itself, not just the worry, including scanning the body, searching symptoms online and pressing on a spot to see if it still hurts. Reducing the checking, not reassurance, is the target.

fields.label: The sensation I am watching
Time and what I was doing when I checked it
How I checked (scan, search, press, ask)
How worried I was before checking (0-10)
How worried right after
How worried an hour later
What I noticed about the pattern this week

title: Continuum Technique
summary: Places an all-or-nothing belief on a 0-100 line with real examples marked along it.
goal: Use it to loosen a two-category belief by finding the graded reality in between.
body_md: Draw a line from 0 to 100 and define both ends in the client’s own words before placing anything on it. Ask for real examples of people or moments that would sit at various points, then place the client’s own situation last. Most clients discover the line has far more room than the original all-or-nothing belief allowed.

fields.label: The all-or-nothing belief
What 0 looks like, specifically
What 100 looks like, specifically
Real examples I can place along the line
Where I placed myself before this exercise
Where the evidence actually places me

title: Time Projection Exercise
summary: Imagines a current crisis from one month, one year and five years in the future.
goal: Use it to loosen the sense that a current problem will feel this large forever.
body_md: Ask the client to genuinely picture each time point rather than rushing to the reassuring answer; some situations will still matter in five years, and that is worth naming honestly too. The value is in noticing which parts of the distress are likely to fade and which are worth acting on now, not in forcing optimism.

fields.label: The current situation and how distressing it is now (0-10)
In one month: what will likely still matter
In one year: what I imagine I will remember
In five years: what place this will have in my life
What this changes about how urgent it feels today
What is still worth acting on now, regardless

title: Chessboard Metaphor
summary: A metaphor placing thoughts and feelings as pieces on a board, with the client as the board itself.
goal: Use it to build a sense of self that holds difficult content without being defined by it.
body_md: Introduce the image slowly: the pieces are fighting for control, but the board itself is never threatened by the fight and does not need any piece to win. Ask the client to notice a recent moment when they were fused with a piece, arguing as if they were the thought, rather than holding the board’s steadier vantage point.

fields.label: The pieces (thoughts and feelings) currently in play for me
Which piece I get pulled into fighting for most
What happens when I fight for that piece to win
What changes when I notice I am the board, not the piece
A recent moment I could have held the board’s vantage point
Where I will practice noticing this during the week

title: Milk Milk Milk Defusion Drill
summary: Repeats a loaded word aloud until it briefly loses its usual meaning.
goal: Use it to give a client a felt, quick demonstration that a word is not the thing itself.
body_md: Say the word milk together for thirty seconds or so and notice what happens to its meaning, then repeat with a milder version of the client’s own difficult word. Choose the first practice word carefully; save the client’s most painful label for once the exercise itself is familiar and trusted.

fields.label: The word we practiced with (start mild)
What happened to the word after repeating it
The word I actually want to try this on
What I noticed when we tried it
A moment this week I could use this quickly

title: Physicalizing the Feeling
summary: Describes a difficult feeling as an object, in size, shape, color, texture and weight.
goal: Use it to build willingness by making an internal feeling something the client can observe.
body_md: Ask the client to locate the feeling in the body first, then describe it as an object rather than judging or naming it. Some feelings shrink under this kind of attention and some do not, and either result is fine; the aim is a description, not a fix. Close by asking if the client is willing to carry the object rather than get rid of it.

fields.label: The feeling and where I notice it in my body
Its size and shape
Its color and texture
Its weight and temperature
What it wants me to do
Am I willing to carry it and act anyway?

title: FEAR and DARE Checklist
summary: Contrasts the FEAR pattern of fusion and avoidance with the DARE moves that counter each one.
goal: Use it to give a client a memorable map from getting stuck to acting on values.
body_md: Fusion, Evaluation, Avoidance and Reason-giving on one side, Defusion, Acceptance, Realistic goals and Embracing values on the other. Work through a recent stuck moment against the FEAR side first so the client recognizes the pattern, then build the matching DARE response for that same moment rather than in the abstract.

fields.label: A recent moment I got stuck
Fusion: the thought I was caught up in
Evaluation: the judgment I added on top
Avoidance: what I did to escape it
Reason-giving: the explanation I gave myself
Defusion and Acceptance: what I could do instead
Realistic goals and Values: what I would be moving toward

title: Workability Log
summary: Rates a recurring action by whether it moves the client toward their values, not by whether it is right or wrong.
goal: Use it to replace judging a coping strategy as good or bad with asking whether it actually works.
body_md: Drop right and wrong from the conversation entirely and ask only whether the action moved the client toward the life they want, in the short term and the longer term. The same action can be workable once and not another time; expect the log to show that rather than a clean verdict.

fields.label: The action I keep returning to
What it costs or gives me in the short term
What it costs or gives me over a week
Does it move me toward my values or away from them?
Is this workable right now, given what matters to me?
What I will try instead, if anything

title: Cope Ahead Script
summary: Rehearses a specific upcoming situation in detail before it happens, including the skills to use.
goal: Use it to reduce vulnerability to a foreseeable difficult moment by planning for it in advance.
body_md: Have the client describe the situation in enough sensory detail to actually feel some of the emotion in session, then rehearse the skills against that felt sense rather than in the abstract. A script rehearsed calmly and vaguely rarely survives contact with the real moment; a script rehearsed against real anticipated distress tends to hold.

fields.label: The situation I am preparing for, in detail
What I expect to feel, and how strong (0-100)
Thoughts I expect to have
The skills I will use, in order
What could get in the way
How I rehearsed it in session

title: STOP Skill Card
summary: Stop, Take a step back, Observe and Proceed mindfully, as a single card to use in the moment.
goal: Use it to interrupt an impulsive reaction long enough for a wiser response to be possible.
body_md: Practice the physical stop first, actually freezing mid-motion in session, since the skill lives in the body more than in the idea of it. Observe means gathering information, inside and out, before choosing anything. Have the client name one real situation this week where pausing changed what happened next.

fields.label: A recent situation where I reacted fast
Stop: what freezing would have looked like
Take a step back: what distance would have given me
Observe: what I would have noticed, inside and out
Proceed mindfully: what I would have done instead
Where I will practice this skill next

title: Self-Soothe Five Senses Menu
summary: A personal list of soothing options for each of the five senses, built ahead of a crisis.
goal: Use it to have concrete, low-effort options ready when distress is too high for problem solving.
body_md: Build this while the client is calm and be specific, a particular scent or song rather than a category, since a vague list gets skipped under distress. Cover all five senses if the client has options for each, and ask where each item actually lives so it is reachable rather than theoretical.

fields.label: Sight: mine are
Sound: mine are
Smell: mine are
Taste: mine are
Touch: mine are
Where each of these actually lives, so I can reach them

title: Half-Smile Practice
summary: A brief relaxed facial expression practiced during a difficult moment, tracked over a week.
goal: Use it to introduce acceptance of a feeling through the body rather than through argument.
body_md: Demonstrate it yourself first, a relaxed, slight expression rather than a full grin, and let the client notice how forcing it feels different from allowing it. This is a small experiment in acceptance, not a way to paper over the feeling, and it works best paired with a few slow breaths rather than used alone.

fields.label: A moment this week I tried it
What I was feeling beforehand
What the half-smile felt like, forced or allowed
What happened to the feeling, if anything
Where I will try it again

title: Accumulate Positives Log
summary: Schedules one small pleasant event most days and one larger values-based goal for the longer term.
goal: Use it to build a buffer of positive experience that makes emotions easier to regulate.
body_md: Keep the short-term events genuinely small and achievable on a bad day, and treat the long-term goal as a separate, slower project rather than something to rush. Clients prone to low mood often let this slip first when things get hard, which is exactly when the buffer matters most; say that plainly.

fields.label: Day
One small pleasant event I did today
How present I was for it (0-10)
A longer-term goal that fits my values
One step toward it this week
What got in the way, if anything

title: Emotional Bank Account Ledger
summary: Each partner logs the small deposits and withdrawals that build or drain trust over a week.
goal: Use it to make the everyday balance of a relationship visible before a crisis forces the conversation.
body_md: Deposits and withdrawals are usually small, a kind word, a dismissive tone, and easy to lose track of day to day. Have each partner keep their own ledger honestly, including their own withdrawals, and compare in session rather than at home where it can turn into scorekeeping.

fields.label: Deposits I made this week, and their effect
Withdrawals I made, even small ones
Deposits I noticed from my partner
Withdrawals I noticed from my partner
My sense of the current balance
One deposit I will make this week

title: Fondness and Admiration List
summary: Each partner writes what they respect and admire in the other, with a specific memory for each.
goal: Use it to rebuild the positive lens on a partner that resentment has narrowed.
body_md: Insist on a specific memory attached to each quality; a list of adjectives with no story behind them does not land the same way. Have each partner read theirs aloud to the other rather than exchanging the sheets silently. Couples deep in conflict often find this the hardest exercise in the set, which is itself useful information.

fields.label: Qualities I admire in my partner
A specific memory for each one
How I usually show this admiration, if at all
What got in the way of writing this
How it felt to hear my partner’s list
One thing I will say to them this week

title: Flooding Recovery Plan
summary: Each partner names their own physical signs of flooding and a self-soothing plan for a break.
goal: Use it to give a couple a shared way to recognize flooding before an argument escalates further.
body_md: Each partner fills this in about themselves, not the other, since flooding looks different for everyone, a racing heart, going blank, wanting to leave the room. Agree the break length and the return signal together, and be clear a break is for calming down alone, not for continuing the argument internally.

fields.label: My physical signs of flooding
What I tend to do or say once flooded
My self-soothing plan during a break
How long my break needs to be
Our signal for calling a break
How we will know it is time to come back together

title: Attachment Styles Match-Up
summary: Each partner identifies their own attachment tendencies and how the pairing shapes their cycle.
goal: Use it to reframe a couple’s pattern as two attachment styles meeting rather than one partner being wrong.
body_md: Introduce the styles as tendencies under stress, not fixed labels, since a client can otherwise use the word as a new way to fight. Ask each partner to describe their own pattern first, in their own words, before naming how it meets the other’s. The pairing itself, more than either style alone, is what predicts the cycle.

fields.label: How I tend to react when I feel distant from my partner
What I need when I am anxious in the relationship
What I need when I want space
How my partner’s pattern meets mine
The cycle this pairing tends to create
One thing I could do differently in that cycle

title: State of the Union Meeting
summary: A weekly structured meeting for a couple to raise what is working and what needs attention.
goal: Use it to give ongoing issues a standing time slot instead of letting them surface mid-conflict.
body_md: Open with appreciation before anything else, every time, even in a hard week. Keep the meeting to a set time and place, and agree that a heated topic gets moved to its own session rather than derailing the meeting. The consistency of the ritual matters more than covering everything each week.

fields.label: Appreciation to open with
What has been working well this week
One issue to raise
What each of us needs about it
One agreement we are making
Anything to carry to next week’s meeting

title: Feelings Collage Poster
summary: The child cuts and arranges pictures of faces and scenes to build a poster of different feelings.
goal: Use it to widen a child’s feelings vocabulary beyond happy, sad and mad.
body_md: Bring old magazines or printed pictures and let the child choose freely rather than assigning categories. Ask what clue in the picture told them the feeling, face, body, situation, as they place each one. The parent hangs the finished poster somewhere the family sees daily and points to it when naming feelings at home.

fields.label: Pictures I chose for happy
Pictures I chose for sad
Pictures I chose for angry
Pictures I chose for scared
A feeling I found harder to find a picture for
Where my grown-up will hang this poster

title: Kindness Rocks Painting
summary: The child paints rocks with kind words or pictures, then decides where to leave or give them.
goal: Use it to build a habit of noticing and offering kindness in a child who is often self-focused by distress.
body_md: Let the child choose the words and colors themselves rather than supplying a list. Ask who each finished rock is for before it is painted, since deciding first tends to make the message more specific. The parent helps the child place or give the rocks during the week and asks afterward how it felt to give one away.

fields.label: Rocks I painted and their messages
Who each one is for
Where or how I gave each one away
How it felt to give one
A kind rock I would like to receive

title: Feelings Puppet Show
summary: The child builds a simple puppet and uses it to act out a feeling and what helps.
goal: Use it to let a child process a feeling through play at a safer distance than talking directly.
body_md: A sock or paper-bag puppet is enough; the point is the distance it gives, not the craft. Let the child choose the puppet’s feeling and story, and follow their lead rather than steering it toward a lesson. The parent watches the show and asks the puppet, not the child directly, what helped it feel better.

fields.label: My puppet’s name
What feeling my puppet has
What happens in the show
What helps my puppet feel better
What my grown-up asked my puppet
Something my puppet’s story is like in real life

title: Star Chart Behavior Tracker
summary: A homemade chart where a child earns a star for one or two specific target behaviors each day.
goal: Use it to increase a specific wanted behavior through immediate, visible recognition.
body_md: Limit it to one or two clearly defined behaviors, described in actions the child can actually do, not general good behavior. The parent awards the star the moment it is earned and says out loud what earned it, rather than saving it for later. Decide the reward for a full row together with the child before starting.

fields.label: The behavior or behaviors we are tracking
How my grown-up will describe it when I earn a star
Day 1-7 stars earned
What I am working toward
How it felt to earn stars this week
What my grown-up noticed changing

title: Emotion Weather Report
summary: The child draws a daily weather picture that matches how they feel, then a forecast for tomorrow.
goal: Use it to build a light, daily habit of naming feelings without pressure to explain them.
body_md: Keep the drawing quick and let the child invent their own weather types, a feeling can be a drizzle or a hurricane in their own words. The parent asks about the picture rather than asking directly how the child feels, since many children find the weather easier to talk about than the feeling itself.

fields.label: Today’s weather (draw or describe it)
What made the weather what it was
What helped, if the weather was stormy
Tomorrow’s forecast
A pattern my grown-up and I noticed over the week

title: Feelings Memory Match
summary: A matching-pairs card game of feeling faces, with a question answered on each successful match.
goal: Use it to build feelings vocabulary through a familiar game rather than direct questioning.
body_md: Make or use a deck of paired feeling faces, face down in a grid, and take turns flipping two at a time. A match is only complete once the player answers a short prompt about that feeling, keeping the game from turning into pure memory recall. Let children retry a hard prompt with help rather than losing their turn.

fields.label: Feelings in our deck
Matches I found
A prompt that was easy to answer
A prompt that was harder
Something I learned about someone else’s answer

title: The Boundary Line Game
summary: Players step forward or back on a physical line to signal comfort with a read-aloud scenario.
goal: Use it to practice noticing and stating a boundary before it comes up in real life.
body_md: Mark a line on the floor and read scenarios aloud, one at a time, having players step toward comfortable or away toward uncomfortable. Ask a few players each round to say the line they would actually use to set that boundary. Keep scenarios everyday rather than the most difficult ones on the first pass.

fields.label: Scenarios we used
Where I stood, and why
A boundary line I said out loud
A scenario where others stood differently than me
What made a boundary easier or harder to state

title: Worry Balloon Pop
summary: Players write a worry on a slip, seal it in a balloon, and pop and address one each turn.
goal: Use it to practice responding to a worry out loud in a playful, low-stakes format.
body_md: Have each player write a real but not-too-heavy worry before the balloons are inflated, and mix in a few silly ones you write yourself to keep the tone light. On each turn, a player pops a balloon and the group offers one thing that might help, then moves on rather than dwelling. End on a note the group chooses together.

fields.label: Worries in our balloons
A worry I popped and what the group suggested
A suggestion I want to actually try
Which worry surprised me
How it felt to say a worry out loud

title: Gratitude Scavenger Hunt
summary: Teams race to find or photograph items matching a list of things to be grateful for.
goal: Use it to practice noticing the positive actively rather than waiting for it to be pointed out.
body_md: Write the list broadly, something that made you laugh, something soft, someone who helped you today, so it fits whatever the group actually has around them. Debrief on which item was hardest to find rather than who finished first; that item usually points at something worth exploring further.

fields.label: Our scavenger list
What I found for each item
The item that was hardest to find
Something I noticed I usually overlook
What I would add to the list next time

title: Feelings Freeze Dance
summary: Players dance to music and freeze in a pose matching a called-out feeling when it stops.
goal: Use it to practice expressing and reading feelings through the body, at a run rather than a discussion.
body_md: Call a feeling just before the music stops so players freeze in a pose for it, then briefly ask a few players what gave their pose away. Rotate who calls the feeling, including children, so the game stays theirs rather than adult-led. Keep the pace quick; the value is in the repetition, not any single round.

fields.label: Feelings we used
A pose I froze in and why
A pose I found hard to read
What clues told us the feeling
A feeling I want to try acting out next time

title: Grounding Anchors Card
summary: A wallet card of the client's own five-senses anchors for coming back to the present.
goal: Give the client a rehearsed way back to the room when the past floods in.
duration: 15 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Build it from things the client actually has to hand: a keyring texture, a scent, a phrase, the feel of their feet. Rehearse it in session while calm and again when mildly activated, so the card is a memory of having done it rather than a set of instructions. Keep it small enough to carry.

fields.label: Five things I can see right now
Four things I can touch, and how they feel
Three sounds I can hear
Two things I can smell or taste
One thing I say to myself: today is (date), I am in (place), I am safe enough
The anchor that works fastest for me
Who I can text once I am back

title: Window of Tolerance Map
summary: A drawing of the client's calm zone, their overwhelmed zone and their shut-down zone, with the signs of each.
goal: Give the client and clinician a shared picture of activation to refer to in every session.
body_md: Draw the three bands together and fill them with the client's own words and body signs. The map earns its place when it becomes a shorthand: the client can say they are near the top edge and you both know what that means. Revisit and widen it as skills build; it is a picture of now, not a fixed trait.

fields.label: Inside my window: how my body and thinking feel when I am okay
Above the window: signs I am revving up (body, thoughts, urges)
Below the window: signs I am shutting down (numb, foggy, far away)
What tends to push me above
What tends to drop me below
What brings me back down from above
What brings me back up from below

title: Trigger and Reminder Log
summary: A week of moments when something in the present set off the past, and what the client did next.
goal: Help the client separate a reminder from the danger it points to, and see their own patterns.
body_md: Frame it as noticing reminders, not reliving events; the log records the cue and the reaction, never the story of what happened. Review it together and look for the sensory reminders the client had not connected before. The final column is where planning happens for next week.

fields.label: Date and where I was
What set it off (a sound, smell, place, phrase, body feeling)
What it reminded me of, in a few words only
How strong the reaction was (0-10) and how long it lasted
What I did in the moment
What helped, even a little
Was there real danger now? What I know about the present situation

title: Safe Place Imagery Script
summary: A written, sensory-rich description of a place, real or imagined, where the client feels calm and in charge.
goal: Give the client a rehearsed inner place to go to at the end of hard sessions and in hard nights.
body_md: Let the client choose the place and check it for hidden reminders before committing to it; a childhood bedroom is often not as safe as it sounds. Build it sense by sense and record the client reading it in their own voice if they want. Use it to close sessions rather than as an exposure exercise.

fields.label: My place, and why I chose it
What I see there, near and far
What I hear
What I feel on my skin, and the temperature
What I smell
Who, if anyone, is with me
The words or image that get me there fastest

title: Container Exercise
summary: An imagined container with a lid where the client puts material that is too much to carry between sessions.
goal: Help the client set things down deliberately at the end of a session instead of carrying them out the door.
body_md: Have the client design the container in detail: what it is made of, how it locks, where it lives. The rule is that what goes in comes back out in session, with you, which is what makes putting it away feel possible. Practice it with something small first so the client trusts the lid before it is needed.

fields.label: My container: what it is made of and what the lid looks like
Where it is kept
How I close it (the words or gesture)
What I am putting in it today
When we will take it out together
What I will do in the ten minutes after closing it

title: Anxiety Body Map
summary: An outline of a body where the client marks where anxiety lives and what it does there.
goal: Turn a vague sense of dread into specific sensations the client can name and watch.
body_md: Draw a simple outline and color it in together; many clients discover they have been calling three different sensations by one name. Ask what each area does first when anxiety starts, because the earliest sign is the most useful one. Return to the map when teaching any body-based skill.

fields.label: Where anxiety shows up first in my body
Where it goes next
What each spot feels like (tight, hot, fluttery, heavy)
The sensation I find hardest
What I usually do when I notice it
One thing I could try instead at the first spot

title: Uncertainty Experiments Sheet
summary: Planned small acts of not checking, not asking and not planning, with predictions to test.
goal: Loosen the belief that uncertainty itself is unbearable by practicing it in small steps.
body_md: Start with experiments that feel about a three out of ten: sending a message without rereading it, ordering without researching the menu. The prediction column is where the learning is, so insist on a specific forecast before each one. Debrief what actually happened, not how it felt.

fields.label: Ways I try to get certainty (checking, asking, over-planning, researching)
This week's experiment: what I will not do
What I predict will happen (be specific)
How sure I am (0-100%)
What actually happened
How the uncertainty felt at the start, and after an hour
What I learned about coping without knowing

title: Avoidance Cost Ledger
summary: A two-column account of what avoiding anxious situations has saved the client and what it has cost.
goal: Make the long-term price of short-term relief visible without arguing with the fear.
body_md: Validate the savings column fully; avoidance works, or nobody would do it. The costs usually appear when the client lists what they have stopped doing over years rather than weeks. Finish by asking which cost they would most like to stop paying, and let that point at the first approach step.

fields.label: Situations I avoid because of anxiety
What avoiding each one saves me in the moment
What it has cost me over the last year
What I have stopped doing altogether
Which cost I most want to stop paying
What a first step back toward it would be

title: Anxiety Wave Timeline
summary: A graph of one anxious episode from first flicker to fade, drawn from memory.
goal: Show the client that anxiety peaks and passes on its own, and where their responses changed its shape.
body_md: Draw the curve together on a timeline with real minutes on it. Most clients have never watched an episode through to the end because they left or distracted at the peak, so mark on the graph where that happened. Repeat with a later episode to show the wave getting shorter.

fields.label: The episode I am drawing (when and where)
First flicker: what I noticed, and the time
Peak: how high (0-10) and when
What I did at the peak
When it started to fade, and what was happening then
How long the whole wave lasted
What I would do differently at the peak next time

title: Paced Breathing Practice Log
summary: A daily record of slow, extended-exhale breathing, practiced when calm so it is there when needed.
goal: Build a breathing habit that lowers the baseline rather than a rescue used only in emergencies.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Teach the pattern in session with a longer out-breath than in-breath, and check that the client is not gulping or straining. The log matters because most clients try breathing once during a spike, find it useless, and give up; practiced twice a day for two weeks it becomes usable. Note the before-and-after ratings, not just the practice.

fields.label: Date and time
The pattern I used (for example in for 4, out for 6)
Minutes practiced
Tension before (0-10)
Tension after (0-10)
Anything that made it hard today
A moment I used it outside practice

title: Values-Based Activity Menu
summary: A menu of small activities sorted by the value each one serves, to choose from on low days.
goal: Give a client with no motivation a list they built while they had some.
body_md: Build it on a better day, because on a flat day the client will not generate options. Sort by value rather than by pleasure, since pleasure is often absent and doing something that matters can come first. Keep every item under twenty minutes and include a few that take two.

fields.label: Values that matter to me (connection, health, learning, creating, helping, order)
Two-minute activities that serve each value
Twenty-minute activities that serve each value
The one I will do tomorrow, and when
What might get in the way
What I will tell myself when I do not feel like it

title: Rumination Interruption Plan
summary: Identifies the client's rumination triggers and plans a concrete switch away from the loop.
goal: Shorten the time spent going over and over the same ground.
body_md: Help the client tell rumination from useful reflection with one question: is this getting anywhere? The switch has to be physical and specific, because a vague plan to think about something else does not survive contact with the loop. Track the triggers for a week before choosing the switch.

fields.label: Where and when I tend to ruminate (bed, commute, shower, scrolling)
The questions that loop (why me, what if, what did I do wrong)
How I feel after an hour of it
The question I will ask to catch it: is this getting anywhere?
My switch: the specific physical thing I will do instead
Where I will put a reminder
How it went this week

title: Small Wins Ledger
summary: A daily record of things done, however small, to counter the mind's report that nothing happened.
goal: Rebuild a sense of capability one entry at a time.
body_md: Set the bar deliberately low and say so: getting up, replying to one message, showering count. The point is evidence against the global verdict that the day was wasted. Read the week's ledger aloud in session; clients often do not believe their own list until they hear it.

fields.label: Date
Three things I did today, however small
One thing that was harder than it looked
Something I did for someone else, or let someone do for me
How I would rate today if I only looked at this list (0-10)
How I was rating it before I wrote it

title: Pleasant Events Bingo
summary: A bingo card of small pleasant activities, marked off through the week for a line or a full house.
goal: Make activity scheduling feel like a game the client can win rather than homework they can fail.
duration: 10 minutes to make, then one week
body_md: Fill the card with the client's own items and a few gentle stretches, with a free square in the middle. A line is a win; a full house is not the goal. In groups, compare cards and trade ideas. The debrief asks which squares turned out better than expected, since anticipation is usually the part that is broken.

fields.label: Squares on my card
The squares I marked this week
The one that turned out better than I expected
The one I could not face, and what got in the way
What I want on next week's card

title: Mood and Energy Rhythm Chart
summary: A week of mood and energy rated at four points a day, to find the client's better hours.
goal: Find the times of day when action is most possible and schedule what matters there.
body_md: Most clients assume the whole day is flat; the chart usually shows a window, often late morning or early evening. Rate mood and energy separately, since they diverge. Use the pattern to move the hardest tasks into the better hours and to plan rest for the worst ones instead of fighting them.

fields.label: Date
Morning: mood (0-10) and energy (0-10)
Midday: mood and energy
Late afternoon: mood and energy
Evening: mood and energy
What I did in my best window
What I will move into that window next week

title: Task Breakdown Ladder
summary: Splits one stuck task into steps so small the first one takes under five minutes.
goal: Get a client past the wall of a task that has no obvious first move.
body_md: Do the breaking-down together in session, since that step is exactly what the client finds hard. Steps should be physical actions, not goals: open the folder, not organize the folder. Have the client do the first rung before leaving the room. Photograph the ladder so it lives on the phone.

fields.label: The task I am stuck on
Why it feels impossible right now
Rungs: every step in order, each under five minutes
The first rung, done now
Where I will keep this ladder
What I will do when I finish a rung (a tick, a break, a message)
When I will do rung two

title: Time Estimate Log
summary: A log of how long the client guessed tasks would take against how long they actually took.
goal: Calibrate the client's sense of time with their own data instead of with reproach.
body_md: Keep the tone curious; the point is a personal correction factor, not proof of failure. Most clients find they underestimate boring tasks and overestimate dreaded ones. Use the ratio to pad plans and to argue with the belief that there is plenty of time.

fields.label: Task
My guess before starting
Actual time (use a timer)
The ratio: actual divided by guess
What I did not count (finding things, getting started, interruptions)
My correction factor for next week's plans

title: Body Doubling Plan
summary: A plan for working alongside another person, in the room or on a call, to get hard tasks started.
goal: Use the presence of another person as external structure for tasks that will not start alone.
body_md: Explain that the double does not help or supervise; they just work nearby. Help the client list who could do this and how to ask without it sounding like babysitting. Plan the first session with a fixed start and stop time and a task chosen in advance, since deciding what to do is itself a stuck point.

fields.label: Tasks I cannot seem to start alone
People who could sit with me (in person or on a call)
How I will ask them
Our first session: when, how long, and what I will work on
What the double will and will not do
How it went, and what I got done

title: Launch Pad Setup
summary: A fixed spot by the door where everything for tomorrow lives, set up with the child each evening.
goal: Take the morning scramble out of the family's day with one predictable place for everything.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then nightly
body_md: Let the child choose the spot and decorate a checklist for it. The parent's job is the evening check-in, not the morning rescue; agree a script for when something is missing that does not turn into a lecture. Review after a week and shrink the checklist to what the child actually forgets.

fields.label: Where my launch pad is
What goes on it every night (bag, shoes, forms, water bottle, gear)
What goes on it only on some days
When we check it together each evening
What my grown-up says if something is missing
How many smooth mornings we had this week

title: Beat the Timer Sprint
summary: A short, timed race against a visible clock to start and finish one small task.
goal: Make starting feel like a game with a finish line instead of an open-ended chore.
body_md: Use a visible timer the child can see counting down, set for less time than the task should take so there is real tension. Play it first with something trivial in session so the rules are learned while the stakes are low. Winning is starting and finishing, not speed; a personal best chart keeps it going at home.

fields.label: The task for this sprint
The timer I set
Did I beat it? By how much
My personal best on this task
What made it fun, and what made it stressful
The next task I want to sprint

title: Triggers, Urges and Alternatives Log
summary: A daily log of what set off an urge, how strong it got, and what the client did instead.
goal: Show the client their own urge pattern and build a list of alternatives that have actually worked.
body_md: Keep it about substance use or the behavior in plain words the client chooses. The strength column shows that urges peak and pass, and the alternatives column becomes a personal menu. Review it without judgment about the days that went badly; the log is data either way.

fields.label: Date and time
What was happening just before (place, people, feeling, time of day)
The urge, and how strong (0-10)
How long it stayed strong
What I did
If I used, what happened next; if I did not, what I did instead
One alternative I want ready for next time

title: Urge Surfing Script
summary: A short guided practice for riding an urge like a wave rather than fighting it or giving in.
goal: Teach the client that an urge is a rising and falling sensation that can be watched.
duration: 10 minutes to teach, then in the moment
body_md: Read it aloud in session while the client recalls a recent urge at low intensity, and narrate the body sensations as they change. The words matter less than the discovery that the urge changed while they watched. Pair with the log so the client can see how long waves really last.

fields.label: Where I feel the urge in my body right now
What it is doing: growing, steady, shifting
The words I use to describe it without judging it
How I breathe while I watch it
What happened to it after two minutes
What I noticed about myself while surfing

title: Recovery Support Roster
summary: A list of the people, places and times the client can lean on, with what each one is good for.
goal: Make support concrete enough to use at eleven at night.
body_md: Sort people by what they are actually good for: company, honesty, a lift, a distraction, someone who has been there. Include groups, lines and places, not just friends. Check that at least two entries are reachable at the client's hardest hour, and have them save the numbers before leaving.

fields.label: People who know about my recovery, and what each is good for
People who do not know, but who are good company
Meetings, groups or places I can go
Numbers I will save today
My hardest hour, and who is reachable then
Who I will tell about a rough patch before it becomes a lapse

title: Playing the Tape Forward
summary: Walks a single urge through to the next morning, so the whole story is present at the moment of choice.
goal: Counter the mind's edit that stops at the first good part.
body_md: Do it out loud, scene by scene, and let the client tell it; the details they add are the ones that will stick. Then write a one-line version for the phone. It works best for a specific plan, not a general resolve, and it pairs with the log's alternatives column.

fields.label: The urge, and what my mind shows me first
Play it forward: the next hour
That night
The next morning
The days after
The one-line version I will keep on my phone

title: Lapse Learning Sheet
summary: A structured look back at a slip: what led up to it, what it meant, and what changes now.
goal: Turn a lapse into information instead of a verdict on the whole attempt.
body_md: Complete it in session soon after the lapse, while the details are available and before shame has rewritten it. The distinction between a lapse and giving up is the heart of it; write that distinction in the client's own words. End with changes to the plan, not promises.

fields.label: What happened, briefly
The hours before: where I was, who with, how I felt
The first small decision that led toward it
What I told myself right before
What I am telling myself now
What this does not mean about me or my recovery
What changes in my plan this week

title: Time-Out Agreement
summary: A written agreement between partners for calling and returning from a pause during conflict.
goal: Let either partner stop a fight before it does damage, without the pause becoming a punishment.
body_md: The return time is the part that makes it work; a time-out with no return is stonewalling with a name. Agree on a word or gesture, a minimum and maximum length, what each partner does while apart, and how they come back. Rehearse the call and the return in session so the first real use is not the first attempt.

fields.label: Our time-out word or signal
How long: minimum and maximum
What I will do during the pause (no rehearsing the argument)
What I will not do (drive angry, drink, text about it)
How we come back: the first sentence
What happens if one of us is not ready at the return time

title: Anger Rules Audit
summary: Lists the client's unwritten rules for how people should behave, and what happens when someone breaks one.
goal: Find the shoulds underneath the anger and decide which are worth the cost.
body_md: Ask for the rules behind three recent flare-ups; they tend to be about respect, fairness and effort. Rate each rule for how often the world breaks it. The question is not whether the rule is right but whether holding it this tightly is worth what it costs the client.

fields.label: A recent flare-up
The rule that was broken (people should...)
How often the world breaks this rule
What holding this rule costs me
A looser version I could live with
Where I will try the looser version this week

title: Cooling Kit Card
summary: A card of physical cooling steps to use in the first two minutes of rising anger.
goal: Give the client something to do with the body before the mouth takes over.
duration: 10 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Choose steps that change physiology: cold water on the face, a long exhale, unclenching the hands, walking. Keep it to four or five so it can be read in a glance. Rehearse in session with a mildly annoying memory and note which step drops the number fastest.

fields.label: Body signs that I am at a six out of ten
My four cooling steps, in order
The one that works fastest for me
Where this card lives
A time I used it this week, and the number before and after

title: Assertive Replay Sheet
summary: Rewrites a recent angry exchange as the assertive version the client wishes they had said.
goal: Build the middle path between exploding and swallowing it.
body_md: Take a real exchange, write what was actually said, then draft the assertive version: the observation, the feeling, the request. Read both aloud and ask which one would have got the client what they wanted. Role-play the assertive line with pushback so it survives a second round.

fields.label: What happened, and what I said
What I actually wanted
The observation, without blame
The feeling, in one word
The request, specific and doable
How I expect them to respond, and my calm reply to that

title: Anger Iceberg Drawing
summary: A drawn iceberg with anger above the waterline and the feelings underneath it below.
goal: Help a child find the hurt, fear or embarrassment that anger is standing in front of.
body_md: Draw the iceberg large and let the child fill the underwater part with feeling words or faces. Use a recent blow-up as the example. Parents can complete one about themselves alongside, which normalizes it and often opens something. Keep the drawing and add to it over sessions.

fields.label: Above the water: what my anger looks like from outside
A time I got really angry
Under the water: what else I was feeling
Which under-water feeling was biggest
What I needed right then
What a grown-up could do when they see my tip of the iceberg

title: Obsession-Compulsion Cycle Map
summary: A drawn loop from intrusive thought to anxiety to ritual to relief and back again.
goal: Give the client a picture of how the ritual keeps the thought coming back.
body_md: Draw it as a circle and let the client supply each stage from a recent example. The relief arrow is the one to linger on: it is the reason the loop persists. Include mental rituals and reassurance seeking, which clients often do not count. Refer back to the map whenever a new ritual comes to light.

fields.label: The thought or image that shows up
What it makes me feel, and how strong (0-10)
What I do to make it go away (including in my head)
How much relief I get, and for how long
How soon the thought comes back
Where on the loop I could try doing something different

title: Ritual Delay Log
summary: A record of rituals postponed by a chosen number of minutes, and what happened to the urge meanwhile.
goal: Introduce the idea of not doing the ritual through delay rather than outright refusal.
body_md: Delay is easier to agree to than stopping and teaches the same lesson. Start with delays of a few minutes on a low-intensity ritual and lengthen them as the client sees the urge drop. Keep the client honest about mental rituals during the delay, since those quietly replace the visible one.

fields.label: The ritual
The urge when it started (0-10)
How long I delayed
What I did during the delay (no mental rituals)
The urge at the end of the delay (0-10)
Did I do the ritual after? What happened either way
Next delay I will try

title: Living With Maybe Practice
summary: Short scripted statements that accept uncertainty about a feared outcome instead of neutralizing it.
goal: Help the client sit with maybe rather than chasing certainty through rituals.
body_md: Write the statements in the client's own words and make sure none of them is a reassurance in disguise; the point is not that it will probably be fine but that they can live without knowing. Practice saying them aloud in session and then use them in place of a ritual, paired with the delay log.

fields.label: The thing I keep needing to be sure about
How I usually get certainty
My maybe statement: maybe it will, maybe it will not, and I can...
What I feel when I say it
When I used it this week instead of a ritual
What I noticed about the uncertainty over the day

title: Family Accommodation Log
summary: A family's record of the ways they take part in rituals, answer for reassurance, or arrange life around the fears.
goal: Show a family how much of the household has bent around OCD, and plan what to step back from first.
body_md: Best completed by the family member, with the client's agreement, and reviewed together. Accommodation is done out of love, so name that before listing it. Choose one small accommodation to withdraw first, agree the exact words the family member will use instead, and expect a harder week before an easier one.

fields.label: Things I do because of the fears (checking for them, answering questions, avoiding places)
Rituals I take part in
How many times a day I am asked for reassurance
What happens when I refuse
The one accommodation we will withdraw first
What I will say instead, in the words we agreed
How the week went

title: Bossy Brain Talk-Back
summary: A child names the part of their brain that gives worry orders and practices talking back to it.
goal: Externalize the intrusive thoughts and rituals so the child and family are on the same side against them.
body_md: Let the child choose the name and draw the character; the sillier the better. Coach parents to use the same name at home so the child is never the problem. Talk-back lines should be short and defiant, and rehearsed in session with you playing the bossy brain giving orders.

fields.label: My bossy brain's name and what it looks like
The orders it gives me
What happens when I obey
My talk-back lines
A time this week I talked back
What my family says to help me boss it back

title: Panic Timeline Sheet
summary: A minute-by-minute account of one panic episode: sensation, thought, action, and what happened next.
goal: Slow a panic episode down enough to see the order of events and where a thought made it worse.
body_md: Reconstruct the most recent episode in session, starting a few minutes before the client noticed anything. Most clients discover a sensation came first and the catastrophic thought second, which is the foundation for everything that follows. Note what they did to escape and what that taught them.

fields.label: Where I was and what I was doing just before
The first sensation I noticed
The first thought about that sensation
What happened in my body next
What I did (sat down, left, called someone, held on)
How long until it faded
What I concluded afterward about my body or the place

title: Body Sensation Practice Log
summary: A record of deliberately bringing on mild panic-like sensations in safe conditions and letting them pass.
goal: Let the client learn from experience that the sensations themselves are uncomfortable but not dangerous.
body_md: Choose the exercises in session with the client's medical situation in mind, and demonstrate each one yourself first: spinning in a chair, breathing through a straw, running on the spot. Rate the sensation and the fear separately. Repetition is the point, so five short practices beat one long one.

fields.label: The exercise and how long I did it
The sensations it produced
How similar to panic (0-10)
How frightening (0-10)
What I did while it faded (no escaping, no safety moves)
How long until it faded
What I learned this time

title: First Sixty Seconds Card
summary: A pocket card with the client's plan for the first minute of a panic surge.
goal: Replace the scramble to escape with a rehearsed sequence the client can do anywhere.
duration: 10 minutes to build, then in the moment
body_md: Keep it to three or four moves that do not involve leaving or checking: feet on the floor, a long exhale, name the sensation, let it crest. Rehearse the sequence in session during a sensation exercise so it is attached to a real feeling. The card is a memory aid, not a safety behavior; retire it once the sequence is automatic.

fields.label: The first sign a surge is starting
Move one
Move two
Move three
What I say to myself as it crests
What I will not do (leave, sit down in the aisle, phone for reassurance)
Where this card lives

title: Sensation Meaning Sheet
summary: Pairs each feared body sensation with the client's frightening explanation and a plainer one.
goal: Weaken the link between a sensation and the catastrophe the client attaches to it.
body_md: List the sensations first, then the meanings the client gives them: a racing heart means a heart attack, dizziness means fainting. Supply plain physiology for the alternative column and check the client actually believes it; if not, that is the next sensation exercise. Rate belief in both columns and repeat over weeks.

fields.label: The sensation
What I fear it means, and how much I believe that (0-100%)
What else it could mean
Evidence from my own history (how many times, what happened)
How much I believe the plainer meaning (0-100%)
The sensation I most want to test next

title: Panic Support Plan for Partners
summary: Agreed roles for a partner or family member during and after a panic episode.
goal: Turn a well-meaning helper from a safety net into a support for facing the episode.
body_md: Partners usually help by escaping together, which keeps the fear alive. Agree in session what the partner will and will not do: stay near, speak little, not leave with the client, not ask if they are okay every thirty seconds. Write the partner's script in their words and rehearse it with both present.

fields.label: What my partner currently does when I panic
What helps in the moment, and what quietly makes it worse
What I want them to do
What I want them not to do
The words they will use
What we will do together afterward
How we will review this after the next episode

title: Repair After Yelling Sheet
summary: A short script for a parent to reconnect with a child after losing their temper.
goal: Make repair the expected next step after a rupture, so a bad moment does not become a bad week.
body_md: Normalize the yelling before planning the repair; a parent drowning in guilt cannot learn. The repair is short, owns the parent's part without self-punishment, and does not extract a promise from the child. Rehearse it in session, then have the parent log one real repair.

fields.label: What happened, briefly
What I was feeling and needing at the time
The repair I will say (in my own words, about a minute long)
What I will not do (over-apologize, explain at length, blame the child's behavior)
When I will do it
How my child responded
What I will do differently at the first sign next time

title: House Rules Builder
summary: A family writes a small set of house rules together, with what happens when they are followed and when they are not.
goal: Make the rules few, positive, visible and agreed, so they can be pointed to instead of argued about.
body_md: Keep it to three to five rules stated as what to do rather than what not to do. Children propose rules for the adults too, which builds buy-in and is usually fair. Consequences are small, quick and related to the rule. Post it somewhere visible and review in a month.

fields.label: Our rules (three to five, said as what we do)
A rule the kids chose for the grown-ups
What happens when a rule is followed
What happens when a rule is broken
Where our rules are posted
The date we will review them

title: When-Then Statement Planner
summary: Rewrites a parent's common commands as when-then statements that make the order of events clear.
goal: Reduce power struggles by stating the sequence instead of the threat.
body_md: Take the parent's three most repeated commands and rewrite each as when the required thing happens, then the wanted thing follows. The tone is matter-of-fact, said once, and then the parent waits. Rehearse the waiting, since that is the hard part.

fields.label: Commands I repeat most
Each one as a when-then statement
How I will say it (tone, once, then wait)
What I will do while I wait
Which one I will use first this week
How it went

title: Parent Trigger Map
summary: Identifies the child behaviors and situations that get under a parent's skin fastest, and why.
goal: Help a parent see their own reactions coming so they can choose a response.
body_md: Ask for the three moments that flip the parent fastest and follow each one to the belief underneath: disrespect, being ignored, feeling judged. Often it links to the parent's own upbringing, and one or two sentences about that are enough. Plan a pause for the top trigger only.

fields.label: The child behaviors that get to me fastest
What each one seems to mean about me or about my child
Where that meaning may come from in my own history
My body's earliest warning sign
My pause for the top trigger
What I will say after the pause

title: Co-Parent Handoff Plan
summary: Agreed steps for handing a child between parents, whether across a house or across two homes.
goal: Take the friction out of transitions so the child does not carry it.
body_md: Works for couples together and for separated parents. Keep the plan about logistics and tone, not about the relationship: what is said at handoff, what is not, how information travels. The child's view of a good handoff is worth asking about separately and including.

fields.label: When and where handoffs happen
What we say to each other at handoff
What we do not raise at handoff
How information about the child travels between us
What our child says makes a handoff easier
Our signal when a handoff is going wrong
How we will review this in a month

title: Sleep and Support Rota
summary: A week's plan for who covers the nights, who covers the mornings, and where a protected block of sleep sits.
goal: Get a new parent one stretch of protected sleep and make the support around them concrete.
body_md: Sleep is the lever that moves most else in the early months, so plan it first. Involve the partner or another supporter in the room if possible. The protected block should be four or five hours, at the same time each night where feeding allows. Note who is on call for each slot and what counts as enough help.

fields.label: My protected sleep block: when, and who covers
Night shifts this week
Morning cover this week
Others who could take a slot (family, friends, paid help)
What I need from a supporter beyond holding the baby
One thing I will stop doing to make room for sleep

title: Intrusive Thoughts After Birth Sheet
summary: Names the unwanted thoughts that arrive with a new baby and separates having a thought from wanting it.
goal: Reduce the shame and fear around intrusive thoughts so the parent can talk about them.
body_md: Ask directly and normalize before the client answers; most new parents have had frightening thoughts and told no one. Distinguish a thought the parent finds horrifying from an intention, and say plainly that horror is a sign of care. Anything the parent describes as a plan or wish needs safety planning in session. Include 988 in the prompts.

fields.label: Thoughts that come that I do not want
What I feel when they come
What I do to make them stop
The difference between having a thought and wanting to act on it, in my words
Who I can tell about these
If things ever feel unsafe: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers

title: New Parent Values Check
summary: A short review of what kind of parent and person the client wants to be, against what the days actually hold.
goal: Reconnect a depleted new parent with what matters, in a form that fits a five-minute window.
body_md: Keep it small; a new parent has no bandwidth for a life review. Three values, three tiny actions. Watch for perfectionism about parenting and name it. The gap between values and days is meant to be noticed with kindness, not closed this week.

fields.label: The kind of parent I want to be, in three words
The kind of person I still want to be, in three words
What my days actually look like right now
One two-minute action for each value
What I will stop expecting of myself this month
Who I will tell about this so they can back me

title: Partner Load Conversation
summary: A structured conversation for partners to lay out the visible and invisible work of a new baby.
goal: Make the mental load visible before resentment does it.
body_md: Have each partner list what they do, including the noticing and planning work, before either comments. Read the lists aloud without defending. The aim is one or two shifts, not a fair split by Friday. Return to it monthly for the first year.

fields.label: Everything I do for the baby and household, including thinking and planning
What I did not know my partner was doing
What I most want taken off my plate
What I could take on
One change we agree for this month
How we will each say when the load tips again

title: Birth Story Reflection
summary: A paced, optional telling of the birth in the client's own words, with the parts they want to keep and the parts they want help with.
goal: Give a parent a way to say what the birth was like, at their pace, and to flag what still hurts.
body_md: Only offer it when the client wants to talk about the birth, and let them stop at any point. Do it in session, not as homework. Listen for what they feel they got wrong, since guilt is common and usually unearned. The last prompt tells you where further work is wanted.

fields.label: What I expected the birth to be like
What happened, as much as I want to say
The moment that stays with me most
What I wish someone had said or done
What I got right
The part I still want help with

title: Self-Critic Voice Profile
summary: Describes the inner critic as a character: what it says, when it shows up, and whose voice it borrows.
goal: Put some distance between the client and the critic so its verdicts can be examined.
body_md: Ask for the critic's exact phrases and tone, then whose voice it sounds like; the answer is often a parent, teacher or ex. Ask what the critic thinks it is protecting the client from, which turns it from an enemy into a misguided guard. Follow with a kinder voice that is firm, not soppy.

fields.label: What my critic says, in its exact words
When it is loudest
Whose voice it sounds like
What it thinks it is protecting me from
What it costs me
What a firm, fair coach would say instead
How I will answer the critic this week

title: Strengths Evidence Bank
summary: A growing file of specific times the client showed a strength, kept as evidence against a harsh self-view.
goal: Collect proof of strengths in a form the client cannot dismiss as flattery.
body_md: The entries must be specific events, not adjectives: the day they stayed calm when the meeting fell apart, not calm. Ask friends and family for entries too, in writing, and add them. Reread the bank before hard things and when the critic is loud.

fields.label: A strength someone else would say I have
A specific time I showed it (what, where, who saw)
A strength I would grudgingly admit to
A specific time I showed that one
An entry from someone who knows me
How I will add to this each week

title: Comparison Detox Log
summary: Tracks the moments the client compares themselves to others, the mood cost, and what they would rather measure themselves against.
goal: Reduce the automatic upward comparisons that drain self-worth, especially online.
body_md: Most comparisons happen on a phone, so the log usually points at a specific app and hour. Ask what the client actually knows about the person they compared themselves to, and what they were comparing: their inside to someone's outside. The alternative measure is against their own last month, not against anyone.

fields.label: Date, place and what I was looking at
Who I compared myself to, and on what
Mood before and after (0-10)
What I actually know about their life
What I was measuring, and whether it is fair
What I would rather measure myself against
One change to when or where I look at this

title: Values Not Verdicts
summary: Replaces global self-ratings with a look at what the client did in line with their values today.
goal: Shift the client from grading themselves as a whole to noticing what they stand for.
body_md: Catch the verdicts first: I am useless, I am a failure. Point out that a whole person cannot be graded like a test, then move to the day's actions and the values they served. This is not a positive rating to replace a negative one; it is a refusal to rate.

fields.label: The verdict my mind hands me most often
What evidence it uses
Three things I did today, and the value behind each
What I would say about a friend who did those things
The verdict, rewritten as a description of an action
One value I will act on tomorrow regardless of the verdict

title: Strength Spotting Circle
summary: Players take turns naming a strength they saw another player use in the session or group, with the evidence.
goal: Practice hearing specific positive feedback and letting it land.
body_md: Go around twice. The speaker must give the evidence, not just the adjective, and the receiver may only say thank you. Watch for deflection and gently stop it. In individual work, play it between client and clinician, taking your turn honestly. Ask afterward which strength surprised the receiver.

fields.label: A strength someone spotted in me, and the evidence
What I wanted to say instead of thank you
A strength I spotted in someone else
The one that surprised me
What I will do with it this week

title: Attention Focus Shift Practice
summary: Trains the client to move attention from monitoring themselves to the person and the room during conversations.
goal: Reduce self-focused attention, which feeds both the anxiety and the sense of performing badly.
body_md: Demonstrate in session: have a two-minute conversation with attention fully inward, then repeat with attention on your face, words and the room, and compare the anxiety ratings. Set graded practices for the week. The log question about what the client noticed in the other person is the proof it worked.

fields.label: The conversation I practiced in
Where my attention was at the start (0 = all on me, 10 = all on them)
What I shifted attention to
Three things I noticed about the other person or the room
Anxiety at the start and at the end (0-10)
What I would have missed if I had stayed inside my head

title: Post-Event Rumination Stopper
summary: A plan for the replay after a social event: what the client will and will not review, and for how long.
goal: Cut short the hours of replaying a conversation and rewriting it as a disaster.
body_md: Explain that the post-mortem is where the day's real damage is done, since it rewrites a fine event as a failure.
